246.title: Don't guess (Avot 1:16)
246.hook: Gamaliel: find a teacher, free yourself of doubt, don't tithe by guesswork
246.howItsDone: Observant Jews in the land of Israel still separate tithes (ma'aser) from produce, and when a question of Jewish law comes up, many ask a rabbi rather than decide by guesswork.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shammai and Abraham's morsel of bread that turned into a feast. Your line was say little, do much. Did anyone get a real smile from you? Day two hundred forty-six.

Dinner with six friends, one check. Somebody says, let's just call it about forty each. Nobody pulls out a calculator. And somewhere at the table, one person who only had soup is quietly paying for someone else's steak, and the person who had the steak is quietly relieved. Nobody meant any harm. It was just a guess. Today's sage worried about exactly that kind of guess, only his table was a farmer's harvest, and the people who went short were the poor.
screen: `ONE CHECK, SIX FRIENDS.` → `LET'S CALL IT FORTY EACH.` → `A HARVEST, AND THE POOR.`

segments.voice: The chain now reaches Rabban Gamaliel, called the Elder. Tradition says he was Hillel's grandson, and he's the first sage the Mishnah calls Rabban, our master. His saying: make for yourself a teacher, remove yourself from doubt, and don't tithe by estimate too often. That last line needs a picture. In the land of Israel, a farmer's harvest had portions that weren't his to keep. Some went to the priests, a tenth went to the Levites, and in certain years a tenth went to the poor. So a farmer stands in front of a heap of grain. He can measure it, or he can eyeball it and say, that's about a tenth. The commentators point out that a guess goes wrong both ways. Too little, and he keeps what belonged to someone else. Too much, and the portion he set aside isn't a proper tithe. Either way, he's living with doubt. Now the first two lines make sense. Make for yourself a teacher. Pirkei Avot already said this, back with Joshua ben Perachyah. Some commentators say that one was about learning, and this one is about decisions: when you don't know, ask someone who does, instead of making it up. And remove yourself from doubt. Don't leave important things resting on a shrug. It's a small, practical saying, and it reaches a long way. Guessing feels easier than measuring. But when other people's share is in the pile, the easy guess costs somebody something.
screen: `RABBAN GAMALIEL THE ELDER.` · `A HEAP OF GRAIN, A TENTH.` · `A GUESS GOES WRONG BOTH WAYS.` · `ASK A TEACHER, LEAVE THE DOUBT.` · then, large: `DON'T GUESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: measure your breath instead of guessing it. Settle, and breathe. Count each breath, in and out as one. Don't estimate. Actually count. One. Two. Three. If you lose track, don't round up. Go back to one. It's harder than it sounds, and that's the point: attention is a kind of measuring. The bell holds the time.
Don't guess. Rabban Gamaliel's rule: find a teacher, step out of doubt, and measure what belongs to others instead of eyeballing it.
Your line: don't guess. Today, measure one thing you'd normally eyeball, a bill, a recipe, a promise of time, especially if someone else's share is in it. Day two hundred forty-six.

247.title: Silence (Avot 1:17)
247.hook: Simeon: I found nothing better for a person than silence
247.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats guarding speech (shemirat halashon) as a serious practice, and some Jews take on periods of deliberate silence, especially during times of reflection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabban Gamaliel and the farmer in front of the heap of grain. Your line was don't guess. What did you measure instead of eyeballing? Day two hundred forty-seven.

Think of the last meeting, or family dinner, where everybody talked at once. Every sentence was louder than the one before, and nobody seemed to be listening. Now think of the one person who said almost nothing, and then, near the end, said one quiet sentence that everybody remembered. Today's sage grew up in rooms like that: rooms full of the most brilliant talkers of his generation. And after a whole life among them, he reported that the best thing he found wasn't a speech.
screen: `EVERYONE TALKING AT ONCE.` → `ONE QUIET SENTENCE.` → `A LIFE AMONG THE SAGES.`

segments.voice: He's Simeon, the son of Rabban Gamaliel from yesterday. He grew up in the house of the leaders of the sages, surrounded by debate. And here is his saying. All my days I grew up among the sages, and I found nothing better for a person than silence. The Hebrew says for the body, as if silence were good for you the way sleep is. Then he adds two lines. Study isn't the main thing; doing is. And whoever talks too much brings on sin. That last line sounds like an old proverb, and it is. In the old King James wording, Proverbs says, "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin." Pile up enough words and something false, cruel or careless is bound to slip in. The Talmud has a saying about this that sounds like a price tag: a word is worth one coin, silence is worth two. And much later in Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Akiva gives the line we're carrying today. A fence around wisdom is silence. Remember the fence around the Torah, from the start of the tractate? A fence doesn't hide what's inside. It protects it. Silence protects what you know from being spilled out carelessly, and it leaves room for what you don't know yet to come in. Notice this isn't a rule against speaking. Simeon's own teachers spent their lives talking about Torah. It's about the weight of words: fewer of them, chosen well, and followed by doing.
screen: `NOTHING BETTER THAN SILENCE.` · `DOING, NOT ONLY STUDY.` · `A WORD IS ONE COIN, SILENCE TWO.` · `A FENCE AROUND WISDOM.` · then, large: `SILENCE IS A FENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: two minutes of real silence. Settle, and breathe. No words, not even in your head, if you can manage it. When a sentence starts forming, a reply, a plan, an argument, just notice it and let it go unsaid. Listen instead. To the room. To your breath. To whatever's under the noise. You don't have to fill the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Silence. Shetikah in Hebrew. Simeon found nothing better for a person, and Rabbi Akiva called it a fence around wisdom.
Your line: silence is a fence. Today, find ten minutes to keep silent on purpose, and in one conversation, let the other person finish before you answer. Day two hundred forty-seven.

248.title: Truth, justice, peace (Avot 1:18)
248.hook: the world endures on three things: truth, justice and peace
248.howItsDone: Jewish teaching treats truthfulness, fair judgment and peacemaking as linked duties, and many Jews learn the three from this saying, which closes the first chapter of Pirkei Avot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon found nothing better than silence, and Rabbi Akiva built a fence out of it. Your line was silence is a fence. Did you find your ten quiet minutes? Day two hundred forty-eight.

Picture a three-legged stool. It's the steadiest seat in the world on uneven ground, as long as all three legs are there. Take one away and it doesn't wobble. It falls. Chapter one of Pirkei Avot started, back with Simon the Just, by naming three things the world stands on: Torah, worship and kindness. Now, at the very end of the chapter, after the whole chain of teachers, another sage names three more. It's as if the chapter ends by building a second stool. Today we sit on it.
screen: `A THREE-LEGGED STOOL.` → `THREE PILLARS, AT THE START.` → `THREE MORE, AT THE END.`

segments.voice: The sage is Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel, and his saying closes chapter one. The world endures on three things: on justice, on truth, and on peace. Then he gives a verse from the prophet Zechariah, which in the old King James wording reads: "execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates." Justice, truth and peace, all in one line of scripture. Notice the difference from the start of the chapter. Simon the Just said what the world stands on, the reasons it exists at all. This saying is about what keeps it going day to day, in courts and markets and kitchens. Commentators love how the three hold each other up. Justice without truth is just power. Truth without peace can be a weapon. Peace without justice is only quiet. There's a teaching in the Jerusalem Talmud that goes further: the three are really one thing, because when real justice is done, truth is done and peace is made. Now today's word. Truth, in Hebrew, is emet. It's spelled with three letters: alef, the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, mem, from the middle, and tav, the very last. The rabbis noticed. Truth runs from beginning to end and holds the middle, they said. And the Talmud calls truth God's own seal, the stamp on everything God makes. That's a lot of weight on one small word. It's also a very ordinary word, the one Hebrew speakers use to say, really? Emet?
screen: `JUSTICE, TRUTH AND PEACE.` · `THE THREE HOLD EACH OTHER UP.` · `EMET: FIRST, MIDDLE, LAST.` · `TRUTH IS GOD'S SEAL.` · then, large: `THE JUDGMENT OF TRUTH AND PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one truth to tell kindly. Settle, and breathe. Think of something true you've been avoiding saying. To a friend, a partner, a boss, a parent. Not a weapon, not a lecture. Just a true thing. Now ask how it could come out with peace in it, too. What would make it fair to them? What would make it gentle? Let the words get simpler and softer with each breath, without letting them stop being true. The bell holds the time.
Truth. Emet in Hebrew: first, middle and last letters of the alphabet, and one of the three things the world endures on, with justice and peace.
Your line: truth, justice, peace. Today, tell one truth in a way that's fair and kind, so all three legs of the stool stay standing. Day two hundred forty-eight.

249.title: Small ones count (Avot 2:1)
249.hook: Rabbi Judah: be as careful with a light commandment as a weighty one
249.howItsDone: Jewish practice gives attention to small commandments as well as great ones, and the command to send away the mother bird (shiluach haken) is often taught as the classic example of a 'light' mitzvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of chapter one: the world endures on justice, truth and peace. Your line was truth, justice, peace. Did you tell one truth kindly? Today, chapter two begins. Day two hundred forty-nine.

You'd run into a burning building for your family. Obviously. But would you hold the door for the stranger with the stroller? Text back your aunt? Put the shopping cart back in the corral when it's raining? Most of us are ready for the big moments. It's the small ones we skip, because surely they don't count for much. Chapter two of Pirkei Avot opens with the man who put the whole Mishnah together, and one of the first things he teaches is about the small ones.
screen: `THE BURNING BUILDING.` → `THE SHOPPING CART IN THE RAIN.` → `THE MAN WHO GATHERED THE MISHNAH.`

segments.voice: He's Rabbi Judah the Prince, so respected that the Mishnah often just calls him Rabbi, as if there were only one. Around the year two hundred, he gathered generations of oral teaching into the Mishnah, the book Pirkei Avot is part of. And here's what he says. Be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, because you don't know the reward that's given for each. Think about that. The Torah has hundreds of commandments, and it almost never tells you what each one is worth. The rabbis say that's on purpose. If you knew the price list, you'd only do the expensive ones. Then they give an example that's hard to forget. In Deuteronomy, if you find a bird's nest with the mother sitting on the eggs, you send the mother away before you take the eggs. It's one of the easiest commands in the Torah. It costs you nothing. And the Torah attaches to it the promise that it will be well with you, and you'll have long days. That's the same promise given for honoring your father and mother, one of the hardest commandments there is. The easiest and one of the hardest, the same reward. So don't sort your good deeds into ones that matter and ones that don't. Rabbi adds a second line, a kind of scale: weigh what a good deed costs you against what it brings, and what a wrong gains you against what it costs. Small things are on that scale too. And you never know which small one is the heavy one.
screen: `RABBI JUDAH, WHO GATHERED THE MISHNAH.` · `NO PRICE LIST FOR THE COMMANDMENTS.` · `THE MOTHER BIRD AND THE PARENTS.` · `WEIGH THE COST AND THE GAIN.` · then, large: `SMALL ONES COUNT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one small one. Settle, and breathe. Let your day come to mind, and look for the tiniest good thing in it you usually skip. Refilling the water jug. Saying thank you to the driver. Answering a message from someone lonely. Pick one. Now picture doing it with full attention, as if it were the most important thing you'll do today. Maybe it is. You don't know. The bell holds the time.
Small ones count. Rabbi Judah the Prince's teaching: treat a light commandment like a weighty one, because nobody knows the reward of each.
Your line: small ones count. Today, do one small good thing slowly and carefully, the kind you'd normally rush past. Day two hundred forty-nine.

250.title: An eye that sees (Avot 2:1)
250.hook: remember three things above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, a book that records
250.howItsDone: Many Jews keep this saying in mind as a reminder that private conduct matters as much as public conduct, and the words 'know before whom you stand' are often written above the ark in synagogues.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Judah the Prince, the mother bird, and no price list for good deeds. Your line was small ones count. Which small one did you do with care? Today, the end of the same saying. Day two hundred fifty.

Everybody drives a little differently when there's a police car in the rearview mirror. And everybody knows the difference between the person they are in public and the person they are alone at eleven at night with their phone. Today's saying is about that gap. It closes the same teaching of Rabbi Judah the Prince we started yesterday. He gives three things to keep in mind so you won't stumble. They're short. You could fit them on a sticky note on your fridge.
screen: `THE CAR IN THE MIRROR.` → `ALONE AT ELEVEN AT NIGHT.` → `THREE THINGS ON A STICKY NOTE.`

segments.voice: Here's how Rabbi Judah ends his saying. Look at three things and you won't come into the grip of sin. Know what is above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book. An eye, an ear, a book. The first picture is being seen. The second is being heard, even the things you say under your breath, and that's the line we're carrying today. The third is being remembered: nothing you do simply vanishes. The prophet Malachi has a picture like this, of a book of remembrance written before God for the people who revere God and think about God's name. Now, this could sound like a security camera, something to make you nervous. But notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say an eye that punishes. It says an eye that sees. The same eye sees the kindness nobody else noticed, and the ear hears the quiet apology, and the book records the small good deed from yesterday too. Being seen can be a comfort as much as a warning. And there's a lovely later reading, from Hasidic teachers, who played with the Hebrew words for know what is above you. They read them as know that what is above comes from you. What happens up there, they said, depends on what you do down here. Your small acts reach further than you think. Either way, the saying closes the gap between the public you and the eleven p.m. you. There's only one of you, and it's seen, heard, and remembered.
screen: `AN EYE, AN EAR, A BOOK.` · `SEEN, HEARD, REMEMBERED.` · `IT SEES THE GOOD TOO.` · `WHAT IS ABOVE COMES FROM YOU.` · then, large: `THE EAR HEARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be seen, gently. Settle, and breathe. Imagine that everything about this moment is noticed, not by a camera, but by someone who wishes you well. Your posture. Your breath. The worry you're carrying. Let yourself be seen that way. Then think of one thing you'll do today when nobody's watching, and picture doing it as if they were. If you pray, you can remember that, in this teaching, God sees and hears. The bell holds the time.
An eye that sees. The first of Rabbi Judah's three: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book.
Your line: the ear hears. Today, notice what you say under your breath, and let it be something you wouldn't mind being heard. Day two hundred fifty.

251.title: Learning and labor (Avot 2:2)
251.hook: study joined with work is good; together they keep wrongdoing away
251.howItsDone: Many Jews combine a profession with regular Torah study, often a set time each day or week, while some communities support full-time study as a calling; both look to sayings like Avot 2:2.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and a book where it's all written. Your line was the ear hears. What did you catch yourself saying under your breath? Day two hundred fifty-one.

There are two ways to get stuck. One person reads every book about changing their life and never changes a thing. It's all ideas, floating. The other works twelve-hour days, head down, and hasn't had a new thought in years. It's all motion, no meaning. Most of us lean one way or the other depending on the season. Today's sage is the son of Rabbi Judah the Prince, the man who gathered the Mishnah. He grew up surrounded by great scholars. And the first thing he tells us is that learning alone isn't enough.
screen: `ALL IDEAS, NO CHANGE.` → `ALL WORK, NO THOUGHT.` → `THE SON OF RABBI JUDAH.`

segments.voice: He's Rabban Gamaliel, the third of that name. His saying: beautiful is the study of Torah together with derekh eretz, because the effort of both keeps sin out of mind. Derekh eretz literally means the way of the land. Elsewhere it means good manners, but here it means earning a living, a trade, the ordinary work of the world. Why would the two together keep wrongdoing away? One reading is simple: a mind busy with learning and hands busy with work don't have much room left for trouble. But there's more. Learning keeps work honest, because you bring what you've learned to the market and the workshop. And work keeps learning honest, because you have to live the ideas with real people and real money. Then Gamaliel gives the warning side. Torah study without work, he says, ends in nothing and brings sin along with it. That's a strong line, and Jews have discussed the balance ever since. The Talmud records two sages who disagreed: one said a person should plow and plant in season and study too, and the other worried that if people are always plowing, when will the Torah get learned? Today, many Jews combine a job with regular study, and some communities support people who study full-time as a sacred calling. Each side reads this saying closely. What they share is Gamaliel's picture: learning and labor aren't enemies. They're two hands, and each keeps the other steady.
screen: `STUDY WITH DEREKH ERETZ.` · `TWO KINDS OF EFFORT KEEP SIN AWAY.` · `EACH KEEPS THE OTHER HONEST.` · `THE SAGES DEBATED THE BALANCE.` · then, large: `LEARNING AND LABOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pair one idea with one task. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've learned recently, anywhere, maybe even from one of these sayings. Careful words. Small ones count. Now think of the work waiting for you today, paid or unpaid. Where could that idea show up in it? In a meeting, a shift, a conversation with a customer or a child. Picture the two meeting. The bell holds the time.
Learning and labor. Rabban Gamaliel's pairing: Torah study with derekh eretz, the work of the world, each keeping the other honest.
Your line: learning and labor. Today, take one thing you've learned and use it at work, and take one question from your work back to something you study. Day two hundred fifty-one.

252.title: His will as yours (Avot 2:4)
252.hook: make God's will your will, so God makes your will His
252.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often describe growth in observance as moving from doing a commandment because it is commanded to doing it with love, and many Jews study this saying as a picture of that change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabban Gamaliel paired Torah with derekh eretz, the work of the world. Your line was learning and labor. Did an idea show up in your work? Today, the same sage goes deeper. Day two hundred fifty-two.

Think about the difference between a kid who cleans his room because he's told to, and the day, years later, when he cleans it because he actually likes a clean room. Same broom. Same floor. But something changed inside. The rule stopped being someone else's and became his. That shift, from have to, to want to, is what today's saying is about. It's one of the boldest lines in chapter two, and it talks about God's will and yours as if they could become the same thing.
screen: `TOLD TO CLEAN THE ROOM.` → `WANTING A CLEAN ROOM.` → `FROM HAVE TO, TO WANT TO.`

segments.voice: Rabban Gamaliel, son of Rabbi Judah, says this. Do His will as if it were your will, so that He will do your will as if it were His. Set aside your will before His will, so that He will set aside the will of others before yours. The Hebrew word for will is ratzon: what you want, what pleases you, your desire. The saying is built like a mirror. Your will and God's will, reflected back and forth. Commentators have read it in more than one way. Some take it very practically: spend on doing good as gladly as you spend on what you want for yourself, and good things will come back to you. Others hear something more inward. At first a commandment feels like someone else's rule. But over years of doing it, you can come to want it, the way the kid comes to want the clean room. Then what God wants and what you want aren't two different things anymore. The second half is harder. Set aside your will. Sometimes what you want and what's good really do pull apart, and the saying asks you to let the good win. It doesn't promise that you'll always get your way. It speaks of God setting aside the will of others, the pressure and plans of people around you, on your behalf. So the carry is simple: want what's good. And it closes a week of sayings: don't guess, silence, truth, justice and peace, small ones count, an eye that sees, learning and labor, and today, his will as yours.
screen: `RATZON: WHAT YOU WANT.` · `A SAYING BUILT LIKE A MIRROR.` · `FROM HAVE TO, TO WANT TO.` · `SET YOUR WILL ASIDE.` · then, large: `WANT WHAT'S GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn one wish toward the good. Settle, and breathe. Let one strong want come up. A thing, a result, a person's approval. Don't push it away. Just look at it honestly. Now ask: is there a good version of this want? Wanting money might hide wanting to care for someone. Wanting to win might hide wanting to be seen. Find the good thing inside, and let the wish lean toward it. If you pray, you can offer that wish to God. The bell holds the time.
His will as yours. Rabban Gamaliel's mirror: do God's will as if it were your own, until wanting and doing the good become one.
Your line: want what's good. Today, when you catch yourself doing something good only because you have to, look for one reason you might actually want to. Day two hundred fifty-two.

pairs: so He does your will as His
so He sets aside the will of others
spend on good as gladly as on yourself

myth: the saying promises you'll always get your way
it asks you to set your will aside, and speaks of God setting aside the pressure of others.
ratzon means will, desire, what pleases you
the saying mirrors God's ratzon and yours.
commentators read this saying only one way
some read it practically, about spending on good; others inwardly, about coming to want it.

fork.setup: you do a good thing every week, but only because you have to. what does Rabban Gamaliel's saying hope for?
options: that you stop, since your heart isn't in it.
that over time you come to want it.
that you keep doing it and never mind why.
fork.reveal: do His will as if it were your will. many teachers read it as the slow change from have to, to want to.

original.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: do His will as your will.

trapdoor: what you thought: do what you're told.
what it means: come to want what's good, until God's will and yours are the same.
what a scholar hears: some commentators read it practically: spend on commandments as freely as on your own desires.
